quote: Beweis dass die 4 Lösungen $f = xy,\ xt,\ yz,$ $zt$, der Differentialgleichung
english: Proof that the 4 solutions f = xy, xt, yz, zt of the differential equation x ∂f/∂x − y ∂f/∂y + z ∂f/∂z − t ∂f/∂t = 0 form the full system of entire rational solutions.
topic: The page concludes a statement that every function of a function field congruent to zero modulo the system of all entire rational functions of the field is an entire algebraic function of them, and begins a proof that xy, xt, yz, zt form the full system of entire rational solutions of the partial differential equation x f_x − y f_y + z f_z − t f_t = 0.

triage.modern_statement: Let the 1-dimensional torus G_m (C*) act linearly on k[x,y,z,t] with weights (1,−1,1,−1), so that λ·(x,y,z,t) = (λx, λ^{-1}y, λz, λ^{-1}t). The operator D = x∂_x − y∂_y + z∂_z − t∂_t is the infinitesimal generator of this action. A polynomial f satisfies Df = 0 exactly when it is invariant, and that happens exactly when every monomial x^a y^b z^c t^d in f has a + c = b + d. The claim is that this ring of invariants (polynomial kernel of D) is generated as a k-algebra by xy, xt, yz and zt, with the single relation (xy)(zt) = (xt)(yz). Geometrically, the quotient is the affine cone over P^1×P^1 (the 'conifold' quadric). This is a worked example in invariant theory, not an open research question.
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's own note claims to prove it, and the result is elementary. It follows from the monomial description: a monomial with a + c = b + d can be split into a product of the degree-2 monomials xy, xt, zy and zt, which is the semigroup/Gordan's-lemma argument for torus invariants. Finite generation of invariant rings in general belongs to Hilbert's 1890 paper 'Über die Theorie der algebraischen Formen' (Math. Ann. 36). Today, computer algebra systems compute invariant rings of tori like this one routinely.

evidence.claim: Gordan's lemma: the lattice points of a rational cone form a finitely generated monoid. For a torus action, invariant monomials are exactly the lattice points of such a cone, so the invariant ring is generated by finitely many monomials.

Hilbert's 1890 paper 'Über die Theorie der algebraischen Formen' (Math. Ann. 36, 473–534) is the foundational work on finite generation in invariant theory. It contains the basis theorem and the syzygy theorem.
Computing invariant rings of linear torus actions given by weight matrices is a standard, implemented routine (e.g. OSCAR's invariant_ring for torus representations).
Background on Hilbert's 1890 invariant-theory paper and its influence.

triage.why: The note proves a specific, elementary fact. The polynomial solutions of x f_x − y f_y + z f_z − t f_t = 0 are the invariants of a C* action with weights (1,−1,1,−1). These are spanned by the monomials with a + c = b + d, and each such monomial factors into xy, xt, yz and zt. This is a textbook example of torus invariants (Gordan's lemma / toric geometry), probably an illustration related to Hilbert's 1890 finiteness work. It is not one of the 23 problems or the 24th problem. The sources above support the general theory; none of them discusses this notebook entry itself, so the link to the 1890 work is my inference, not something a source states.
